  "text": "The tide came in an hour early. By the time Mara noticed, water had covered the stepping stones and lifted the old fishing boat from its bed of sand.

Her father’s watch said six. The church clock, faint across the estuary, agreed. Only the sea insisted otherwise.

She stood on the jetty with a bag of groceries and watched a pair of shoes drift past, neatly tied together by their laces. They were brown leather, polished despite the salt water. Her father had owned a pair like them.

Behind her, the boat knocked against the pilings.

It had not floated in eleven years.

Mara set down the groceries. An orange rolled free, stopped at the edge, then slipped into the rising water. She expected it to drift toward the harbor. Instead, it circled the boat once and vanished beneath the hull.

From inside the cabin came three measured taps.

She knew that knock. Every evening of her childhood, it had sounded against her bedroom door before her father entered to say goodnight.

The water reached her ankles.

Across the estuary, the church bell began striking seven, though its last note of six seemed hardly to have faded.

Mara stepped aboard. The deck yielded under her weight, and she caught the cabin door to steady herself. On the brass latch she found a fresh smear of blue paint, the same color her father had been using the morning he disappeared.

She wiped it with her thumb.

Inside, someone pulled out a chair. Its wooden feet scraped slowly across the floor."

  "text": "At closing time, the library returned a book to itself.

Clara watched it slide through the brass slot and land on the counter. Outside, snow lay undisturbed beneath the door. She had locked it twenty minutes ago.

The book was small, bound in green cloth, and warm enough to mist her glasses when she bent over it.

There was no title.

Inside the front cover, someone had pasted a borrowing card. Every line bore her name, written in the careful hand she had abandoned after primary school. The dates began tomorrow and continued for forty years.

The last entry had been crossed out.

Clara turned to the first page.

It described the library exactly: the broken radiator, the fern dying above the catalog drawers, her wet scarf hanging from a chair. At the bottom, a single sentence recorded something she had not yet done.

She looked toward the history shelves.

A man stood there holding his hat.

Clara shut the book.

“I haven’t read that far,” she said.

The man lowered his eyes. Snow melted on his shoulders, falling onto the carpet without leaving a mark.

“Neither have I.”

She recognized his voice from a message she had saved for nine winters, though he looked younger than her brother had ever been.

Between them, the book opened with a soft crack of glue.

Several pages fluttered past. Clara pressed her palm against them, trying to hold her place.

Her brother stepped closer.

“Before you read any more,” he said, “tell me whether you want me to stay.”

Under her hand, the next page was already turning."

  "text": "On Tuesday, the sea delivered a wardrobe.

It stood upright on the beach below Mara’s house, its mirrored door facing inland. The tide withdrew around its feet without wetting the wood.

Mara took a kitchen knife down to the shore.

She had lived alone long enough to distrust gifts that required two people to carry.

The wardrobe smelled of lavender and railway smoke. Inside hung a single yellow coat, a child’s size, with a shell in each pocket.

She knew the coat. She had sewn the crooked buttonholes herself.

Behind her, someone cleared their throat.

A little girl stood barefoot in the shallows.

“You’re supposed to knock,” the girl said.

Mara gripped the knife by its blade before noticing and turning it around.

“Where did you get that face?”

The girl touched her cheek, puzzled.

“It came with me.”

For thirty years, Mara had imagined what her daughter might look like: first with missing teeth, then taller, then tired from work. This was the face she had never needed to imagine.

The girl pointed to the wardrobe.

“I left something.”

Mara lifted the coat from its hanger. Beneath it was a damp envelope addressed in her own handwriting.

She opened it.

There were only six words.

Don’t let her take you swimming.

The girl was watching her now.

“Who wrote that?” she asked.

Mara folded the letter and put it in her pocket.

“Someone who knows me.”

She held out the coat. The girl stepped into it, lifting her hair away from the collar just as Mara remembered.

Together they struggled with the buttons while the water crept up the beach."
